primitives.name: In-Game Win Probability
primitives.verbatim_quote: INTRODUCTION In-game win probability models provide the likelihood that a certain team will win a game given the current state of the game.
primitives.assumptions: Binary outcome assumption, Markovian state transitions, stationary opponent ratings.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Late-game scenarios with extreme score gaps (>25 pts) and short time-to-go (<60 seconds).

layer2.mapping: Bayesian updating framework for dynamic scoring rate analysis.
layer2.telemetry: Posterior calibration error vs. bookmaker implied odds.

primitives.name: Simple Linear Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: Clearly the result of the game was not the one projected at that point and hence, critiques of these models appeared.
primitives.assumptions: Constant linear relationships between game-state features and win probability.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Nonlinear decay of time-value near game end (t → 0+), leading to catastrophic miscalibration.

layer2.mapping: Conformal prediction intervals for uncertainty quantification.
layer2.telemetry: R-squared drop below 0.5 for endgame drives.

primitives.name: Logistic Regression
primitives.verbatim_quote: In particular, we build a logistic regression model that utilizes a set of 10 variables to predict the running win probability for the home team.
primitives.assumptions: Multivariate normality of predictors, linear log-odds relationship, independence of observations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Overfitting in sparse data regions (e.g., >20 pt deficits with <2 min remaining).

layer2.mapping: Bayesian logistic regression with Laplace priors for feature selection.
layer2.telemetry: Cross-validation AUC < 0.65 for extreme deficit scenarios.

primitives.name: Drive Length Analysis
primitives.verbatim_quote: During Super Bowl 51, late in the third quarter the probability assigned by some of these models to New England Patriots to win was less than 0.1% or in other words a 1 in 1,000 Super Bowls comeback [7].
primitives.assumptions: Stationary drive efficiency across quarters, constant yards-per-play expectation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Structural breaks in drive distribution due to defensive substitution patterns.

layer2.mapping: Hidden Markov Models for drive-state transition probabilities.
layer2.telemetry: Residual heteroskedasticity in drive yardage predictions.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core failure mode of NFL win-probability models stems from treating game dynamics as a static linear transformation of state variables. This reduces the problem to a logistic regression over summary statistics, ignoring the sequential nature of downs and field position. When teams face fourth downs with long yardage to go, the linear model assumes a constant conversion probability, whereas in reality, aggressive playcalling introduces heavy-tailed distributions in remaining yards. Additionally, the assumption of independent increments leads to severe miscalibration in the tails; for instance, a 20-point deficit with 3 minutes left should not imply a win probability of zero, but rather a small but finite chance of a turnover followed by a touchdown drive. The simple linear model fails because it does not account for the non-Markovian nature of football scoring, where the history of timeouts and red-zone efficiency significantly alters future prospects.
